---
title: "Moving from NACHO 2"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

NACHO 3 stores a study in one `nacho` object, where NACHO 2 used a list with a long `$nacho` table.
This article is for you if you have NACHO 2 code, saved NACHO 2 objects, or a pipeline that calls NACHO 2.
It shows how to convert your objects, which calls change, and which results change.

You do not have to move.
NACHO 2.0.8 keeps working with the code you have.
If you stay, pin the version, for example with `renv::install("NACHO@2.0.8")`.
NACHO 3 needs R 4.3 or newer.

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| message: false
library(NACHO)
```

## Saved objects

A NACHO 2 object saved with `saveRDS()` does not work as a NACHO 3 object.
`read_nacho()` reads a saved file from any NACHO version, and converts NACHO 2 objects on the way.
`upgrade_nacho()` converts an object that is already in your R session.

```{r}
#| label: upgrade-call
#| eval: false
old <- readRDS("nacho-2-object.rds")
nacho <- upgrade_nacho(old)

nacho <- read_nacho("nacho-2-object.rds")
```

The conversion keeps the raw counts, the sample sheet, the settings and the thresholds.
It computes the quality-control metrics, the normalised counts, the PCA and the outlier flags again, with the NACHO 3 definitions.
It also moves the object to the legacy preset with `background = "geo", background_mode = "subtract"`, so the flags and the background correction stay close to what NACHO 2 gave you.
The numbers can still differ slightly, because of the changes listed in the section on results.
Only read files you trust, since `readRDS()` can run code stored in a file.

`read_nacho()` also reads NACHO 3 objects, and `upgrade_nacho()` returns a NACHO 3 object unchanged.
`GSE74821` is already a NACHO 3 object, so this call changes nothing.

```{r}
#| label: upgrade-noop
identical(upgrade_nacho(GSE74821), GSE74821)
```

## From NACHO 2 to NACHO 3

The table gives the NACHO 3 call for each NACHO 2 call.
Read `x` as a `nacho` object.

| NACHO 2 | NACHO 3 |
|:--------|:--------|
| `x$nacho`, the long table | `as.data.frame(x, long = TRUE)`. |
| The `Count` column of `x$nacho` | `nacho_counts(x)`, a matrix with one row per probe and one column per sample. |
| The `Count_Norm` column of `x$nacho` | `nacho_counts(x, normalised = TRUE)`. |
| The sample columns of `x$nacho` | `nacho_samples(x)`, one row per sample. |
| The probe columns of `x$nacho` | `nacho_probes(x)`, one row per probe. |
| `x$outliers_thresholds` | `nacho_thresholds()` builds a set of limits, and `x@thresholds` holds the ones in use. |
| The `is_outlier` column of `x$nacho` | `nacho_qc(x)[["status"]]`, with one status per metric, `n_flags` and `reason` beside it. |
| `check_outliers()` | Removed, since the status always follows the thresholds of the object. |
| `normalise(x, remove_outliers = TRUE)` | `exclude_outliers(x)`. |
| `autoplot(x, x = "BD")` | `autoplot(x, type = "BD")`. |
| `render(x, output_file = , show_outliers = , clean = )` | `render(x, format, output_dir, title, author, group)`. |
| `visualise(x)`, which saved `nacho_object.rds` in `tempdir()` | `visualise(x)` returns the tuned object, and writes no file. |
| `deploy()`, which defaulted to `/srv/shiny-server` | `deploy(directory = )`, with no default. |

NACHO 2 had no `x$raw_counts` and no `x$normalised_counts`, although some old documentation said so.
The raw and normalised counts were the `Count` and `Count_Norm` columns of `x$nacho`.

### Counts and tables

`nacho_counts()` returns a matrix, so the long table is no longer the way in.
`as.data.frame(x, long = TRUE)` gives the long layout back when you need it for ggplot2 or `dplyr`.

```{r}
#| label: accessors
dim(nacho_counts(GSE74821))
dim(nacho_counts(GSE74821, normalised = TRUE))
dim(as.data.frame(GSE74821, long = TRUE))
```

In NACHO 2, `x$nacho` repeated the sample columns on every probe row.
In NACHO 3, `nacho_samples()` and `nacho_probes()` keep them apart.

### Outlier flags

`nacho_qc()` gives one row per sample.
Each metric has its own status column, and `status`, `n_flags` and `reason` sum them up.
The limits come from `nacho_thresholds()`, and `x` keeps them, so there is no `check_outliers()` to run.

```{r}
#| label: qc
head(nacho_qc(GSE74821)[, c("IDFILE", "status", "n_flags", "reason")], n = 3)
```

`exclude_outliers()` drops the flagged samples and normalises the others again.
`normalise()` has no `remove_outliers` argument any more.
When no sample is flagged, `exclude_outliers()` says so and returns the object.

```{r}
#| label: exclude
nacho <- exclude_outliers(GSE74821)
dim(nacho_counts(nacho))
```

### Plots

`autoplot()` takes the plot name in `type`.
NACHO 3 stops when you pass `x`, and the error names the new argument.

```{r}
#| label: autoplot
#| fig-alt: "Binding density of the 48 samples of GSE74821, one point per sample."
autoplot(GSE74821, type = "BD")
```

```{r}
#| label: autoplot-old
#| eval: false
autoplot(GSE74821, x = "BD")
#> Error: `x` was renamed `type` in NACHO 3.0.0.
```

### Reports

`render()` writes a Quarto report, and the old arguments are gone.
`output_file` and `clean` have no replacement: the file is `nacho-report.html` or `nacho-report.pdf` in `output_dir`, and the working files live in a temporary folder.
`show_outliers` has no replacement either.
The report settings `outliers_factor` and `outliers_labels` still change how flagged samples look.
The report needs the Quarto command-line interface 1.9.18 or newer.
Use `format = "typst"` for a PDF, which needs no LaTeX.
`render()` returns the path of the report.

```{r}
#| label: render
#| eval: false
path <- render(
  GSE74821,
  format = "html",
  output_dir = "reports",
  title = "Quality control of GSE74821",
  author = "Jane Doe, Genomics Core"
)
```

The first argument is `x`, not `nacho_object`, so name it only when you use the new name.
`title`, `author` and `group` are new.
With `group`, which names a column of `nacho_samples(x)`, the report checks whether the batches and the biological groups are confounded.

### The app

`visualise()` opens the app and returns the tuned object when you click **Done**.
`nacho_app()` returns a Shiny app object, and `deploy()` writes a one-line `app.R` next to the app files.
`deploy()` no longer defaults to `/srv/shiny-server`, so pass `directory`.
Read [Explore quality control in the app](nacho-app.html) for a tour of the pages.

```{r}
#| label: visualise
#| eval: false
tuned <- visualise(GSE74821)
deploy(directory = "/srv/shiny-server")
```

## Results that change

The same data can give different numbers in NACHO 3.
These changes come from corrections of the methods, not from the new class.

- The PCA is computed again with the NACHO 3 code, so the components can differ.
- Normalised counts are no longer rounded, and no longer floored at 0.1.
- There is no background correction by default, which is `background = "none"`.
  Choose a statistic with `background` and whether to threshold or subtract with `background_mode`.
  Subtracting floors the counts at 0.
- Samples are flagged against the nSolver thresholds by default, where NACHO 2 used its own limits.
- Negative probes are excluded with Bruker's rule, which drops at most two probes that are 3-fold above the others.
- The positive control linearity leaves out POS_F and adds 1 to every count in the nSolver preset.
- `Negative_factor` is always the geometric mean of the kept negative controls, also with `normalisation_method = "GLM"`.
  NACHO 2 subtracted the model intercept, so GLM-normalised counts differ.
  The background applied sits in the new `Background` column.
- `housekeeping_predict = TRUE` picks the five most stable genes by geNorm, among the genes above background in at least 90% of the samples.
  NACHO 2 picked the five genes with the smallest spread.
- miRNA panels are no longer normalised with housekeeping genes by default.
  Give `housekeeping_genes`, or set `housekeeping_norm = TRUE` or `housekeeping_predict = TRUE`, to turn it back on.
- Plots use the NACHO theme, and the shared labels use US spelling, such as "Normalized" and "Hemolysis".

## NACHO 2 outlier calls

The legacy preset keeps the NACHO 2 limits.
With `background = "geo", background_mode = "subtract"`, it gives back the NACHO 2 outlier calls.
A converted object already has these settings.
For a NACHO 3 object, pass them to `normalise()`.

```{r}
#| label: legacy
legacy <- normalise(
  GSE74821,
  outliers_thresholds = nacho_thresholds(preset = "legacy"),
  background = "geo",
  background_mode = "subtract"
)
table(nacho_qc(legacy)[["status"]])
```

For new data, give the preset to `load_rcc()`, with `preset = "legacy"`.
The limits of the preset are the NACHO 2 defaults, the ones stored in `x$outliers_thresholds`.

```{r}
#| label: legacy-limits
str(nacho_thresholds(preset = "legacy"), max.level = 1)
```

## Pipelines

The nf-core/modules modules `nacho/qc` and `nacho/normalize`, which `nf-core/nanostring` uses, call NACHO 2 code.
They read `$nacho`, and call `autoplot(x = )` and `render(output_file = , show_outliers = )`.
All three fail in NACHO 3.
The modules pin NACHO 2.0.6, so they keep working until they update.

| Module call | NACHO 3 replacement |
|:------------|:--------------------|
| `x$nacho` | `as.data.frame(x, long = TRUE)`. |
| `autoplot(x, x = "BD")` | `autoplot(x, type = "BD")`. |
| `render(x, output_file = "report.html", show_outliers = TRUE)` | `render(x, output_dir = "reports")`, which writes `reports/nacho-report.html`. |

Rename or move the report in the next step of the pipeline if it expects another file name.

The `NEWS.md` file lists every breaking change by source file.
